identity.title: Discernible phenotypic alterations following linc-10 knockout in Caenorhabditis elegans.

content.abstract: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) are regulatory molecules that play vital roles in various cellular processes. Although the loss of function of most annotated lncRNAs in several model organisms does not result in severe phenotypes, suggesting they are not essential for survival or reproduction, lncRNAs may still act as responsive elements under diverse physiological and pathological conditions. In this study, we investigated the role of the linc-10 gene in Caenorhabditis elegans and found that its deletion is associated with altered gene expression and impaired reproductive fitness. Knockout (KO) mutants of linc-10 exhibited mild but notable abnormalities, including reduced brood size, altered developmental trajectories, and increased sensitivity to stress, along with occasional sterility and a slightly elevated male ratio. We characterized the expression patterns of linc-10 across developmental stages and performed high-throughput sequencing to detect differentially expressed genes (DEGs) following linc-10 deletion. We found that several immune-related genes were dysregulated. Notably, linc-10 mutants showed increased susceptibility to Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14 infection and other stressors. Small RNA sequencing further revealed alterations in piRNA and miRNA profiles after linc-10 deletion. Importantly, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated insertion of a Plinc-10::linc-10 rescue transgene into a neutral intergenic site partially rescued the reduced brood size and stress-sensitive phenotypes of linc-10 mutants, supporting the functional relevance of the linc-10 transcript. Together, these findings suggest that linc-10 contributes to reproductive fitness, immune homeostasis, and stress resilience in C. elegans.
